The WHO guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery, and monitoring emphasize the integration of nutrition throughout the life course to improve health outcomes for individuals living with HIV. 2. Operational guidance on HIV and infant feeding in emergencies highlights the importance of breastfeeding duration and the role of health services in supporting optimal feeding practices among mothers living with HIV. 3. Updated recommendations on HIV and infant feeding focus on the duration of breastfeeding and the provision of health service support to enhance feeding practices for HIV-positive mothers. 4. General care for individuals living with HIV includes managing common coinfections and comorbidities, with specific reference to WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behavior. 5. WHO emphasizes that every movement contributes to better health, underscoring the importance of physical activity for individuals living with HIV. 6. Essential prevention and care interventions for adults and adolescents living with HIV in resource-limited settings are outlined in WHO guidelines, including the use of antiretroviral therapy (ART). 7. The IMAI district clinician manual provides guidance on hospital care for adolescents and adults with limited resources, focusing on the management of illnesses in HIV-positive individuals. 8. WHO guidelines on post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV and the use of co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for HIV-related infections provide a public health approach to reducing infection risks among adults, adolescents, and children. 9. Studies have demonstrated the survival benefits of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in HIV-positive adults, including those in resource-limited settings such as Oromiya, Ethiopia, and Jinja, Uganda. 10. Research in Mozambique highlights the long-term treatment outcomes of adults enrolled in a rapidly expanding ART program, emphasizing the importance of sustained care. 11. Co-trimoxazole preventive therapy has been shown to reduce mortality when initiated alongside ART in South Africa, particularly in severely immunosuppressed individuals. 12. Failure to prescribe pneumocystis prophylaxis in the cART era is associated with increased mortality, as evidenced by data from the Treat Asia HIV observational database. 13. Clinics offering co-trimoxazole prophylaxis in Malawi report lower early mortality rates among patients receiving ART, highlighting the importance of integrated care. 14. Severely immunocompromised HIV-infected patients in Cambodia have shown positive responses to highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), underscoring the need for timely treatment initiation. 15. Supplementary feeding for wasted Malawian adults initiating ART has demonstrated health benefits, emphasizing the role of nutritional support in HIV care. 16. Daily co-trimoxazole prophylaxis in severely immunosuppressed HIV-infected adults in Africa has been associated with reduced mortality and hospital admissions, as shown in the DART cohort analysis. 17. A systematic review and meta-analysis confirm the efficacy of co-trimoxazole prophylaxis in reducing morbidity and mortality among HIV-positive adults, including pregnant women. 18. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis and ART have been shown to significantly reduce mortality and hospital admissions in HIV-infected Zambian children. 19. The impact of co-trimoxazole on causes of death, hospital admissions, and antibiotic use in HIV-infected children has been documented, highlighting its role in pediatric HIV care. 20. Discontinuation of co-trimoxazole prophylaxis in HIV-infected Ugandan adults with CD4 counts >200 cells/μL increases the risk of malaria and diarrhea, emphasizing the need for continued prophylaxis. 21. A randomized trial in Kenya demonstrated the safety and efficacy of discontinuing co-trimoxazole prophylaxis in ART-treated HIV-1-infected adults, provided virological suppression is achieved. 22. Prolonged co-trimoxazole prophylaxis in HIV-infected children in Africa has been shown to reduce morbidity and mortality, as evidenced by a randomized trial. 23. Discontinuing primary pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis in virologically suppressed HIV patients with CD4 counts <200 cells/μL remains a clinical challenge, as highlighted in observational studies. 24. A systematic review and meta-analysis confirm the safety of co-trimoxazole use during pregnancy, supporting its role in preventing opportunistic infections in HIV-positive pregnant women. 25. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for HIV-exposed but uninfected infants has been shown to reduce morbidity and mortality, as demonstrated in randomized controlled trials in Botswana and South Africa. 26. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis has been associated with increased resistance gene prevalence and changes in gut microbiome diversity among HIV-exposed infants, raising concerns about long-term microbial health. 27. The protective efficacy of co-trimoxazole prophylaxis against malaria in HIV-exposed children in Uganda has been demonstrated in randomized clinical trials. 28. Prolonged co-trimoxazole prophylaxis up to age 4 years has shown efficacy in preventing malaria in HIV-exposed children in Uganda, as evidenced by open-label trials. 29. The efficacy and safety of different malaria prevention regimens in young HIV-exposed Ugandan children have been evaluated, with co-trimoxazole showing significant benefits. 30. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of community-acquired pneumonia in children emphasize the importance of early detection and treatment, particularly in HIV-endemic regions. 31. Predictive models suggest that co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for children born to HIV-positive mothers can significantly reduce mortality up to the age of two years. 32. Consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection provide a public health approach to improving outcomes for individuals living with HIV. 33. WHO guidelines on tuberculosis (TB) prevention and control emphasize the integration of TB and HIV care, particularly in resource-constrained settings. 34. Empirical TB therapy versus isoniazid preventive therapy in advanced HIV patients initiating ART has been evaluated in multicountry trials, with significant implications for early mortality prevention. 35. Systematic or test-guided treatment for TB in HIV-infected adults has been shown to improve outcomes, as demonstrated in randomized controlled trials. 36. The overlap between HIV and multidrug-resistant TB epidemics necessitates integrated care strategies, as highlighted in systematic reviews and meta-analyses. 37. Isoniazid preventive therapy combined with ART has been shown to reduce TB incidence in HIV-positive individuals, as evidenced by randomized controlled trials. 38. Long-term follow-up of the Temprano trial in West Africa demonstrates the mortality reduction benefits of isoniazid preventive therapy in HIV-infected adults with high CD4 counts. 39. Treatment of latent TB infection in HIV-infected individuals remains a critical component of care, as outlined in Cochrane reviews and WHO guidelines. 40. Clinical characteristics and outcomes of HIV patients admitted to intensive care units in Africa highlight the need for specialized care in resource-limited settings. 41. The fixed-dose combination of tenofovir, lamivudine, and dolutegravir (TLD) has been recommended for HIV treatment, with evidence supporting its efficacy and safety. 42. WHO guidelines on TB infection prevention and control provide updated recommendations for reducing transmission in healthcare and community settings. 43. The global hepatitis report and WHO strategies emphasize the integration of viral hepatitis care into HIV programs to achieve better health outcomes. 44. Progress reports on HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections highlight the need for accountability in implementing global health sector strategies.
